drills.q: An RL agent's reward goes up steadily during training but the real-world task success metric stays flat. Name the phenomenon and the first thing you check.
drills.a: Reward hacking / a mis-specified proxy reward. First check: does the reward function actually correlate with the true objective on a few hand-picked known-good vs known-bad trajectories, and log the true metric alongside raw reward from run 1.

drills.q: Your manager wants to use full RL to optimize a news feed's click-through rate. What's your first diagnostic question, and what do you expect the answer to imply?
drills.a: Does the action taken now (which items shown) change the distribution of contexts/users seen next in a way the objective cares about? For most feed ranking it doesn't, implying this is a contextual bandit, not full RL — simpler, more stable, no real credit-assignment problem.

drills.q: Explain why RL training data violates the i.i.d. assumption that most ML theory relies on.
drills.a: The agent's own policy determines which states/actions are visited, and the policy itself is being updated during training, so the data-generating distribution changes as a direct consequence of learning — it is neither independent (states are causally linked along a trajectory) nor identically distributed over time.

drills.q: A single-frame Atari observation is fed to a policy network and performance is inexplicably noisy specifically on tasks requiring motion judgment. Diagnose.
drills.a: The state isn't Markov — one frame can't recover velocity/direction, so perceptually identical frames with different histories require different correct actions and the network can't distinguish them. Fix: frame-stacking or recurrence to approximate the belief state.

drills.q: Explain the deadly triad and why tabular Q-learning is safe from it despite being off-policy and bootstrapped.
drills.a: Function approximation + bootstrapping + off-policy learning together can cause divergence with no convergence guarantee. Tabular Q-learning has no function approximation — updates touch only the single (s,a) entry with no generalization bleeding error into unrelated states — so only two of the three legs are present, which is provably safe.

drills.q: Design the reward for a warehouse robot task-assignment system in one sentence, then name one exploitable gap in it.
drills.a: E.g. -1 per timestep, +100 per completed task, penalty for collisions. Exploitable gap: the robot can repeatedly complete trivial nearby tasks to farm completion bonuses while ignoring a hard, high-value task sitting in the queue, since the reward doesn't distinguish task difficulty or priority.
